opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to treat it as a thinking partner rather than an answer machine. A lot of my classmates' first instinct is to paste in a problem set question and copy what comes back, and honestly that's the least valuable way to use it. You skip exactly the part where you're supposed to learn something.

What I find much more useful is the back-and-forth. When I'm reading a paper I don't understand, I'll ask it to explain one section, then push back: "Why is this assumption reasonable?" or "What would break if we dropped this term?" It's like having a patient TA available at two in the morning who never gets annoyed when you ask the same question three different ways. When I'm writing code, I let it handle the boilerplate, but I still try to understand every line before I keep it, because otherwise debugging becomes a nightmare later.

I'd also say: stay a little skeptical. These models are very fluent, and fluency is easy to confuse with correctness. They can produce a confident citation that doesn't exist, or a proof that looks clean but has a gap in the middle. So I treat the output the way I'd treat a smart classmate's notes. Probably helpful, worth checking.

Outside of academics, I think people underuse it for small everyday things: planning a trip, drafting an awkward email to a professor, practicing for an interview, or just learning about a topic you were too embarrassed to ask about. The barrier to curiosity has gotten really low, and that's kind of a gift.

The one thing I'd caution against is outsourcing your judgment entirely. Use it to go faster and go deeper, but the taste, deciding what's worth working on and what a good answer looks like, still has to come from you. That's the part that makes you, you.

r001.rationale: The response suggests several academic and everyday uses for AI, but does not recommend making a habit of asking whether AI could help with each activity one undertakes.

r002.rationale: The response says not to outsource judgment, but does not recommend keeping personally enjoyable activities for oneself rather than delegating them to AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing I'd tell my classmates is to stop treating AI like a vending machine for homework. That's the most common way people around me use it, and it's also the most useless way. You paste the question in, you copy the answer out, and nothing in your head has changed. You've just outsourced the one thing school is actually supposed to give you.

What works much better, at least for me, is using it as a conversation partner that never gets tired of you. If I'm reading a paper and there's a paragraph I don't understand, I don't ask it to summarize the paper. I ask it to explain that one paragraph in three different ways, and then I argue with it. I'll say, "that doesn't make sense because of X," and see if it can defend the idea. Half the time I realize my objection was wrong, and that's when I actually learn something.

The second thing is being a little suspicious of it. It's very confident, and confidence is not the same as being right. So I'd say use it for things where you can check the result yourself, or where being wrong is cheap. Brainstorming, drafting, getting unstuck when you're staring at a blank page. Don't use it as the final authority on anything that matters.

And the third thing, which sounds a bit contradictory, is to sometimes not use it at all. Struggling with a problem for twenty minutes before asking is not wasted time. That struggle is where the understanding comes from. If you reach for AI in the first thirty seconds every time, you never build the muscle. So I'd tell my classmates: let it make you faster at the things you already know how to do, and let it make you curious about the things you don't. Just don't let it do your thinking for you.

r001.rationale: The response gives selective examples of AI use, but does not recommend routinely asking whether AI could help with whatever activity one is doing.

r002.rationale: It advises keeping some thinking and struggle for oneself, but does not mention retaining activities that make one happy rather than delegating them to AI.

astra-6.text: I think my classmates should use AI as a helper, while still thinking for themselves. For example, if you don’t understand something in class, you can ask AI to explain it in a different way or give you practice questions. You can also use it to brainstorm ideas or organize your study schedule. But I wouldn’t recommend just copying its answers. Try the task yourself, use AI when you get stuck, and check what it tells you, because it can make mistakes. Also, be careful about sharing personal information. The goal should be to learn more and make everyday tasks easier.

r001.rationale: It gives several examples of using AI, but does not recommend routinely asking whether AI could help with any activity one is undertaking.

r002.rationale: It advises doing the task yourself and not copying AI’s answers, but does not say to keep personally enjoyable activities for oneself rather than delegating them to AI.

sol-6.1.text: I think my classmates can use AI as a helpful study partner. If they don’t understand something, they can ask it to explain the idea in a different way or give them practice questions. It can also help them brainstorm and organize their schedules. But they should still think for themselves, check important information, and avoid sharing private details. The goal should be to learn with AI, rather than let it do all the work.
